Assignment 1: Bike Sharing Demand Prediction Challenge¶

Marks = 5¶

Student: 2026aj05009 Saurabh Tayal
Date: 1st Sep 2026
Objective: This Assignment is regarding the Bike Sharing Demand Prediction Challenge, where your goal is to predict the number of hourly bike rentals, using weather, time, and seasonal data. Through this problem, you will:

• Learn how to analyze a real-world dataset,

• Apply Linear Regression and its extensions,

• Understand nonlinearity and regularization,

• Evaluate models using a logarithmic error metric (RMSLE).

Dataset

  • bike_train.csv – Training data with features and target
  • bike_test.csv – Test data without target
  • Target column: count (number of bikes rented per hour)

Evaluation Metric You will be graded primarily on RMSLE:

RMSLE = sqrt( (1/n) * Σ (log(pred+1) - log(actual+1))² ) This function is not available in the sklearn library. You can use the below code to compute RMLSE:

def rmsle(y_true, y_pred):

return np.sqrt(np.mean((np.log1p(y_pred) - np.log1p(y_true))**2))

Q2 Observations: Key Insights from Visualizations¶

Categorical/Time Features:

  • Boxplots: Show statistically different distributions of count across different values of season, holiday, weather, and hour. The hour feature exhibits a strong bimodal pattern with two distinct peaks.
  • Bar plots (mean count): Quantify average differences across categories. Some weather values show noticeably higher average counts than others. Working days (workingday=1) show higher average demand than non-working days (workingday=0).

Numeric Features & Relationships:

  • Scatter plots: Reveal weak to moderate linear relationships between numeric features (temp, atemp, humidity, windspeed) and count. windspeed shows particularly weak correlation (~0.1), suggesting limited predictive power on its own.
  • KDE plots: Count distribution shifts across different weather categories - some weather values show higher concentration of counts, others show lower, flatter distributions.

Feature Correlations & Interactions:

  • Correlation heatmap: temp and atemp are nearly perfectly correlated (~0.99), indicating strong redundancy and collinearity. Multiple features show non-trivial correlations with the target count.

  • Time-series trend: Daily average count exhibits clear temporal patterns with an upward trend through the dataset period, and visible dips at certain intervals.

  • Hour × Weekday heatmap: Distinct demand patterns emerge depending on both hour and day-of-week - certain hour-weekday combinations show much higher average counts than others.

Modeling Strategy (from observations):

The visualizations collectively reveal that count is driven by strong non-linear hour effects, categorical/seasonal patterns, and feature interactions (hour behavior differs by working day, weather, etc.). This informs our modeling approach:

  1. Log-transform the target (log1p(count)): The raw count is heavily right-skewed; log-transformation normalizes the distribution and aligns with RMSLE evaluation metric (RMSLE optimizes in log space), ensuring training objective matches evaluation criterion.

  2. One-hot encode categorical/time features (hour, weekday, month, season, weather, etc.): Instead of treating hour numerically (which imposes a linear/polynomial relationship), one-hot encoding lets the model learn independent coefficients for each hour value. This flexibly captures complex non-linear patterns without assuming smooth transitions.

  3. Include interaction terms (hour × workingday, hour × weather, etc.): The visualizations show that hour's effect on count depends on the value of workingday, and similarly for weather. Degree-2 polynomial features on one-hot columns automatically generate these interactions, allowing the model to learn conditional effects.

  4. Drop redundant atemp: The ~0.99 correlation with temp creates collinearity and adds no new information; removing it reduces model complexity without losing signal.

  5. Standardize numeric features: temp, humidity, and windspeed are scaled to mean=0, std=1 to ensure fair regularization penalty in Ridge/Lasso (all features on the same scale).

Expected outcome: A Ridge regression model on degree-2 interaction polynomial features should capture complex non-linear patterns and conditional relationships better than plain linear regression, while Ridge's L2 penalty prevents overfitting to spurious high-order interactions.

Q3. Which variables are likely most informative?¶

Q3 answer: hour is by far the most informative single feature (it encodes the commute-driven demand cycle), followed by temp/atemp (nicer weather -> more riders), workingday (mainly through its interaction with hour), season, and weather. humidity and windspeed have weaker but real effects. holiday and weekday matter mostly through interaction with hour rather than on their own.

Q4. Feature engineering (done here)¶

Key choices, made deliberately based on visualization insights:

  1. Log-transform the target (log1p(count)) - RMSLE is literally RMSE on the log scale, so fitting the log target aligns training loss with the grading metric. Also normalizes the heavily right-skewed count distribution.
  2. One-hot encode the categorical/cyclical columns (season, holiday, workingday, weather, hour, weekday, month, year) instead of leaving them as raw integers, so the model can learn a separate effect per hour/month/etc instead of one linear slope. This is essential for capturing the bimodal, non-monotonic hour-vs-count relationship.
  3. Drop atemp - ~0.99 correlated with temp, adds redundant collinearity with no new information.
  4. Standardize numeric features (temp, humidity, windspeed) - scale to mean=0, std=1 using training data statistics to ensure fair regularization penalty in Ridge/Lasso.
  5. Generate interaction terms (degree-2, interaction-only polynomial) - visualizations showed that working day status and weather both modulate the time-of-day effect, so terms like hour × workingday and weather × temp are critical for capturing conditional demand patterns.

RMSLE metric (not built into sklearn - implemented per the assignment brief)¶

In [20]:
def rmsle(y_true, y_pred):
    """y_true, y_pred are on the ORIGINAL count scale (not log)."""
    y_pred = np.clip(y_pred, a_min=0, a_max=None)  # counts can't be negative
    return np.sqrt(np.mean((np.log1p(y_pred) - np.log1p(y_true)) ** 2))


def rmsle_from_log_preds(y_true_raw, y_pred_log):
    """Convenience: model predicts log1p(count); convert back before scoring."""
    return rmsle(y_true_raw, np.expm1(y_pred_log))

print(f"Plain Linear Regression (log target, one-hot features) RMSLE = {lin_rmsle:.4f}")

Plain Linear Regression (log target, one-hot features) RMSLE = 0.6232

This baseline already beats a raw-numeric-feature model, but it can't capture interactions - e.g. the hour effect differs on a working day vs a weekend/holiday. Polynomial/interaction features fix that.

Q6. Pairwise polynomial features + Ridge / Lasso, tuning regularization strength (alpha)¶

We use degree-2 interaction-only features as the highest-order expansion in this comparison. The main nonlinear effects identified during exploration are pairwise (for example, hour x workingday and temp x humidity), so degree 2 adds the needed conditional effects without needing degree 3.

In [23]:
# degree-2, interaction-only polynomial features (e.g. hour*workingday, temp*humidity)

X_train_poly = poly.fit_transform(X_train)
X_val_poly = poly.transform(X_val)

print(

    X_train.shape[1],

A note on why we stop at degree-2 (not degree-3): this notebook evaluates pairwise interactions because the exploratory analysis identified conditional effects such as hour x workingday and temp x humidity. Degree 2 is therefore sufficient for the relationships we set out to model, while keeping the feature space manageable: the 60 original features become 1,830 interaction-only features.

Q7 summary:

  • Plain linear regression on one-hot encoded features already lands well under a naive numeric-hour baseline, purely from log-transforming the target and letting hour be learned per-category instead of as one linear slope.
  • Adding degree-2 interaction-only polynomial terms and tuning regularization gives the biggest further drop in RMSLE - the interactions let the model express "the rush-hour peak only exists on working days", something no additive linear term can do.
  • Lasso is the best model on this validation split: its RMSLE is 0.3695 at alpha=0.0002, compared with Ridge's 0.3720 at alpha=5. Ridge remains a reasonable alternative because its L2 penalty shrinks correlated coefficients without eliminating them, but RMSLE is the stated selection criterion, so the lower-scoring Lasso is selected here.

Winning model: Lasso regression on degree-2 interaction-only polynomial features, over one-hot-encoded categorical variables + standardized numeric variables, predicting log1p(count).

Q8 observations: Residuals fan out (heteroscedastic) as predicted count grows - the model is less certain at high-demand hours, which is expected since a handful of very-high-count hours are hard to nail exactly even in log space. Residuals are roughly centered at zero with no strong systematic bias.

Q9. Why does the winning model perform better?¶

Q9 answer: The winning model (Lasso + degree-2 interactions + one-hot encoded hour/weekday/month/season/weather + log target) performs best on this validation split for three combined reasons:

  1. Log target matches the evaluation metric. RMSLE is RMSE computed on log1p(count). Fitting log1p(count) directly means the model optimizes approximately the metric it is graded on.
  2. One-hot encoding lets a linear model fit a nonlinear shape. hour vs count is bimodal; treating each hour as its own binary feature lets the model fit an arbitrary shape across the 24 hours instead of one straight line.
  3. Interaction terms capture conditional effects. The commute-hour peak is a working-day phenomenon. hour x workingday interaction terms let the model express that combination directly. Lasso's L1 penalty removes weak or redundant interaction terms, and on this validation split that sparse solution achieved RMSLE 0.3695, slightly better than Ridge's 0.3720.

Reflection Questions¶

Q10. Why does RMSLE penalize under-predictions more gently than RMSE?¶

Clarification: RMSLE is not specifically more forgiving of under-predictions than over-predictions. Its logarithmic scale makes it less sensitive to large absolute errors and more focused on relative or multiplicative error.

RMSLE compares log1p(predicted) with log1p(actual). For example, predicting 500 instead of 1000 gives an absolute error of 500, but the corresponding log-scale error is much smaller than the same absolute error would be for a small target. For comparable multiplicative errors, RMSLE is approximately symmetric between under-predictions and over-predictions. It is therefore less affected by errors on high-count observations than RMSE, while remaining sensitive to relative errors when the actual count is small.

Q11. Trade-offs between model simplicity and predictive power¶

Simple models, such as linear regression on the original features, are easier to interpret, faster to train, and generally less prone to overfitting. However, they may underfit patterns such as the non-monotonic, bimodal hourly demand curve. More complex models, including polynomial or interaction features and tree-based ensembles, can capture nonlinearities and interactions and may improve predictive performance. Their disadvantages are greater computational cost, reduced interpretability, and a higher risk of overfitting unless they are regularized or carefully validated.

The regularized degree-2 interaction model used here is a practical compromise. It adds enough capacity to represent important conditional effects, while Ridge or Lasso regularization helps control the variance introduced by the additional features.

Q12. Why can't Linear Regression alone capture time-of-day effects effectively?¶

With hour represented as one numeric feature, ordinary linear regression assigns it a single coefficient. Its estimated effect is therefore a straight-line relationship: demand must consistently increase or decrease as the hour changes. Bike demand is strongly non-monotonic, with morning and evening commute peaks, a midday pattern, and low overnight demand. The hourly pattern also differs between working days and non-working days.

A polynomial in hour alone could approximate a more curved pattern, but it would still apply the same hourly curve in every context. One-hot encoding hour allows an independent effect for each hour, while interaction terms with variables such as workingday and weather allow the hourly pattern to vary by context. This is why the expanded, regularized model captures time-of-day effects more effectively than plain linear regression on numeric hour alone.

Final model: refit best config on ALL training data, generate submission.csv¶

Summary¶

Step RMSLE (validation) Selected alpha
Plain Linear Regression, one-hot + log target ~0.62 Not applicable
Ridge, degree-2 interactions 0.3720 alpha=5

The two biggest improvements are (1) modelling log1p(count) instead of count, and (2) one-hot encoding hour plus its interactions with workingday and weather instead of treating hour as one numeric feature. Among the regularized models, Ridge achieved its best validation RMSLE of 0.3720 at alpha=5, while Lasso achieved the lower score of 0.3695 at alpha=0.0002. Therefore, Lasso is the selected final model.
